title: Career Roadmap: Network Technician
summary: A Network Technician installs, configures, monitors and maintains computer networks that allow devices, servers and applications to communicate. The role involves working with routers, switches, wireless access points, network cables, firewalls and network monitoring systems.

about.label: Industry
about.text: IT Services, Telecommunications, Networking, Cloud Infrastructure and Enterprise IT

about.label: Workplaces
about.text: IT companies, telecom operators, data centres, hospitals, banks, educational institutions, network service providers and government departments

about.label: Career Type
about.text: Technical support, network installation, troubleshooting and infrastructure maintenance

blocks.text: A Network Technician installs, configures, monitors and maintains computer networks that allow devices, servers and applications to communicate. The role involves working with routers, switches, wireless access points, network cables, firewalls and network monitoring systems.
ECE diploma graduates can enter this career by combining their electronics fundamentals with practical knowledge of computer networking, IP addressing, network devices and troubleshooting.

Fresh graduates commonly start as Network Support Trainee, Junior Network Technician, IT Support Technician, NOC Technician or Field Network Technician. Advanced network engineering and administration roles generally require additional experience and specialized skills.

items.text: Install and maintain LAN, WAN and Wi-Fi infrastructure.
Connect computers, printers, servers and network devices.
Configure basic network settings and IP addresses.
Assist with router, switch and wireless access-point configuration.
Diagnose connectivity, cabling, DNS and DHCP problems.
Monitor network availability and respond to alerts.
Test Ethernet cables and troubleshoot physical-layer faults.
Maintain network diagrams, asset inventories and configuration records.
Escalate complex routing, firewall and security incidents.
Follow access-control, cybersecurity and change-management procedures.
Support network upgrades, device replacements and infrastructure installations.
Communicate service issues and resolutions to users and senior engineers.

Primary pathway

items.text: Complete Class 10.
Enrol in a recognized Diploma in Electronics & Communication Engineering.
Study digital electronics, communication systems, computer fundamentals and networking.
Learn TCP/IP, IP addressing, switching, routing, DNS, DHCP and wireless networking.
Practise in a networking lab using simulators and available physical equipment.
Complete an internship or supervised project involving network installation or troubleshooting.
Apply for entry-level network support, NOC, IT support or field technician roles.

blocks.text: Alternative pathway

Candidates can also pursue a B.E./B.Tech in Computer Science, Information Technology, Electronics & Communication or a related field. A degree may broaden eligibility for some graduate-level positions, but many technician roles prioritize practical skills and role-specific qualifications.
The following plan assumes a three-year diploma. Adapt it to the actual curriculum and duration of the programme.

items.text: Understand the OSI and TCP/IP models.

blocks.text: Practical skills

items.text: Configure basic switch and router functions in a lab.
Understand VLANs, trunk links and basic routing.
Troubleshoot DNS, DHCP, gateway and cabling issues.

rows.text: Understand how devices communicate across networks

Understand gateways, routing tables and basic routing concepts

blocks.text: A Network Technician should develop knowledge in the following areas:

blocks.label: LAN and WAN
blocks.text: Local and wide-area network concepts.

blocks.label: IP addressing
blocks.text: IPv4, subnetting and an introduction to IPv6.

blocks.label: Switching
blocks.text: MAC address tables, VLANs and trunking.

blocks.label: Routing
blocks.text: Static routing and introductory dynamic-routing concepts.

blocks.label: Wireless networking
blocks.text: Wi-Fi deployment, signal issues and access-point troubleshooting.

blocks.label: Network services
blocks.text: DNS, DHCP, NAT and NTP.

blocks.label: Network security
blocks.text: Firewall concepts, secure device access and access-control lists.

blocks.label: Network monitoring
blocks.text: Availability, latency, packet loss, bandwidth and device health.

blocks.label: Physical infrastructure
blocks.text: Structured cabling, patch panels, racks and cable testing.

blocks.label: Cloud networking
blocks.text: Basic virtual networks, subnets, routing and security groups.

rows.text: Simulate routers, switches and network topologies
PuTTY or an equivalent terminal client

Diagnose IP configuration and connectivity issues

Maintain IP inventories, asset lists and incident logs

blocks.text: Start with simulators and virtual labs. Access physical devices only with permission and follow the organization's change-control procedures.
Network Technicians may be evaluated on:

items.text: Time taken to acknowledge and resolve assigned incidents.
Accuracy of troubleshooting and escalation.
Network availability and connectivity within their responsibility.
Successful completion of installation and maintenance tasks.
Compliance with approved configuration and change procedures.
Accuracy of network diagrams and asset inventories.
Repeat-incident rate.
Quality of user communication and ticket documentation.
Compliance with security policies and access controls.

blocks.text: Performance measures vary by employer and should not encourage unsafe or unauthorized network changes.
For every project, document the problem statement, topology, IP-addressing plan, configuration, test results, limitations and security considerations.
Use this scale to assess readiness:

items.text: 1: Beginner
2: Basic awareness
3: Can perform supervised tasks
4: Can perform routine tasks independently within authorization
5: Advanced competence

blocks.text: The target levels are learning goals, not a formal certification or employment assessment.

blocks.text: What to learn during an internship

items.text: Network installation and structured cabling.
Device inventory and network diagram maintenance.
Basic IP configuration and connectivity troubleshooting.
DNS and DHCP fault diagnosis.
Switch and access-point installation under supervision.
Ticket handling, incident escalation and user communication.
Network monitoring and routine maintenance.

blocks.text: Try to gain practical experience with both physical infrastructure and logical network configuration. Do not make changes to production networks without authorization.

blocks.text: The strongest long-term approach is to combine networking fundamentals with troubleshooting, automation and security awareness.
By the end of the diploma, aim to demonstrate:

items.text: A recognized Diploma in Electronics & Communication Engineering.
Strong understanding of TCP/IP, subnetting, switching and routing fundamentals.
Ability to configure basic IP settings and diagnose common connectivity faults.
Familiarity with DNS, DHCP, VLANs and wireless networking.
Practical experience using Packet Tracer and Wireshark.
Basic Windows and Linux troubleshooting skills.
At least two documented networking projects.
Internship or supervised field exposure, where available.
A technical resume listing real lab exercises and project outcomes.
Preparation for networking fundamentals, aptitude and troubleshooting interviews.

blocks.text: For an ECE diploma student, the most practical route into network technology is to learn networking fundamentals, practise in a lab, build troubleshooting projects and gain hands-on experience.

Start by targeting Network Support Trainee, IT Support Technician, NOC Technician or Junior Network Technician roles. Once comfortable with IP addressing, VLANs, routing, network monitoring and incident management, pursue a relevant certification such as CCNA and progress toward network administration, cloud networking or network security.
The key differentiator is not just knowing networking theory—it is being able to diagnose a fault methodically, document the solution and restore service without introducing additional risk.
